reading.passage:
When a municipal library began lending tools, its managers expected drills to prove most popular. Instead, the longest waiting list was for devices that detect damp behind walls. The original procurement plan had classified these devices as specialist equipment. Residents, however, used them to document problems that landlords had attributed to poor ventilation, sometimes without visiting the property.

The library refused to certify the readings. Its staff could explain how to operate a device, but could not judge whether a building was defective. This distinction frustrated some borrowers, who argued that an institution capable of issuing a device should stand behind its conclusions. Yet removing the meters from circulation would have deprived residents of an inexpensive way to decide whether to seek professional advice.

The pilot's success is therefore difficult to express as a count of transactions. A meter that circulates twice may matter more than a hammer borrowed every weekend, provided it helps someone formulate an informed question. The managers have retained measures of use, while asking borrowers separately whether access changed what they were able to do next.

questions.prompt: Why does the author mention the original procurement classification?
options: To argue that specialist devices should remain in professional hands.
To show that assumptions about likely users missed a practical demand.
To imply that library staff had deliberately suppressed information.
To explain why damp meters were more expensive than drills.
questions.explanation: The label had not anticipated ordinary tenants' use of the devices.

questions.prompt: What position does the library take on the measurements?
options: It accepts them only when corroborated by a landlord.
It uses them to decide whether a property requires inspection.
It teaches operation without endorsing the interpretation.
It certifies only readings taken with staff present.
questions.explanation: Operational guidance is expressly separated from a judgment on the building.

questions.prompt: Why might two meter loans matter more than many hammer loans?
options: Some loans enable decisions or questions that raw counts do not capture.
The meters have to circulate more slowly because they need maintenance.
Frequent hammer users have a higher risk of damaging the equipment.
Meters are judged primarily by how much money borrower fees generate.
questions.explanation: The passage assesses what a loan makes possible, not just circulation.

questions.prompt: What is the author’s overall position on transaction counts?
options: They should be discontinued because they distort branch comparisons.
They become reliable only once the library verifies every outcome.
They are suitable only for measuring demand for common tools.
They are useful but incomplete without evidence of what access enables.
questions.explanation: The managers retain usage measures and supplement them.

listening.transcript: We used to put every donated item on the catalogue as soon as it arrived. That created an illusion of abundance. Three sewing machines were listed, for example, but one lacked a pedal, another had no instructions, and a third could only be used safely after an induction. So we changed what the catalogue promises. An item now appears as available only when it can be used independently, or when we can supply the support needed to make that possible. The number of listings fell sharply, which worried our funders. But failed collections almost disappeared. I would rather have a modest catalogue that people trust than an impressive one that quietly transfers all the troubleshooting to the person standing at the desk.

questions.prompt: What did the original catalogue exaggerate?
options: The number of donated sewing machines.
The reliability of items listed as usable.
The experience of library employees.
The frequency of public enquiries.
questions.explanation: The inventory existed, but some items could not readily be used.

questions.prompt: When can an item now appear as available?
options: Only if every borrower has already completed an induction.
Only if it was acquired directly from the manufacturer.
When it is independently usable or suitable support can be provided.
When it can be repaired during the borrower’s first visit.
questions.explanation: The new policy permits either independent use or accompanied support.

questions.prompt: What concern did funders express indirectly through their reaction?
options: The smaller catalogue looked like a decline in provision.
Safety training had become too demanding.
The library was refusing too many donations in advance.
Public demand for sewing machines had collapsed.
questions.explanation: They worried after seeing fewer listings, even though reliability improved.

questions.prompt: What does 'transfers all the troubleshooting' imply?
options: Repairs were officially contracted to the desk staff.
Users were already experts at diagnosing equipment failures.
Donors had to remain available to support borrowers.
The former system left borrowers to absorb difficulties the library had not resolved.
questions.explanation: The phrase exposes work hidden by the impressive-looking inventory.

writing.prompt: Should public libraries lend equipment as well as books? Explain the strongest case for and against expansion.
writing.followup: Suggest one indicator of success that a library could use without asking borrowers to disclose personal details.
writing.model: Libraries should lend selected equipment when occasional access matters more than ownership. A damp meter or a sewing machine can help people make an informed decision without committing money to a purchase. The obvious objection is operational: broken tools, missing accessories and safety training can absorb staff time that is already scarce. I would protect the core collection by giving a small pilot a separate budget and accepting only items that can be maintained locally. To assess it, the library could offer one anonymous question at return: did this loan let you complete a task or decide what to do next? Responses would measure practical benefit without asking what the task was, where it happened or whom it involved.

speaking.prompt: Describe one item your local library could lend that would benefit several groups of residents.
speaking.followup: What borrowing rule would make the scheme fairer?
speaking.model: I’d start with an inexpensive electricity monitor. A tenant could work out whether an old heater is consuming more power than expected, while a school group could use the same device for a project on household energy. I’d avoid making demand difficult to see by offering the monitor only during office hours. Instead, I’d introduce a seven-day limit and a waiting list. If nobody is waiting, the borrower can renew once. That balances two needs: people get enough time to compare their readings, but one enthusiastic borrower cannot keep the device all winter.

reading.passage:
A city commissioned a study to establish which bus stops offered the least protection from summer heat. The first maps ranked stops by the percentage of tree canopy within a twenty-metre radius. On paper, a stop beside a hospital garden scored well. The field team, however, found that the pavement where passengers queued was in direct sun throughout the afternoon; the trees shaded an adjoining service road.

The researchers then measured the time that shade actually reached the waiting area. Their revised maps changed the order in which sites were treated. Engineers objected that data collected on a handful of afternoons could not represent every season. The researchers agreed, but argued that the relevant question was narrower: where could passengers wait during the hottest period without being exposed continuously?

The city ultimately planted trees at several stops and installed removable canopies at others. This was not a rejection of tree-cover data. Those figures were retained for longer-term planning, where the question was which neighbourhoods lacked vegetation, rather than which passengers stood in the sun. One measurement had been asked to answer two different questions.

questions.prompt: Why did the stop near the hospital initially rank well?
options: Its queues were shortest during the hottest hours.
Its shelter had been designed for summer conditions.
Its temperature was lower than that of nearby stops.
Its score reflected nearby trees that did not shade the queue.
questions.explanation: The canopy radius included trees shading another surface.

questions.prompt: What distinction did the researchers use to answer the engineers?
options: Potential winter risk was more important than immediate summer exposure.
The field measurements addressed a particular period and location.
The tree-cover figures were too inaccurate for any planning purpose.
A larger field team could eliminate seasonal variation.
questions.explanation: The investigators deliberately narrowed the question rather than claiming full seasonal representation.

questions.prompt: What does retaining tree-cover figures imply?
options: They remain useful for a different decision at a wider scale.
They would be used instead of ground observations in later summers.
They matter only where removable canopies cannot be fitted.
They were kept solely to avoid admitting a procurement error.
questions.explanation: The broad vegetation picture still guides neighbourhood planning.

questions.prompt: What lesson does the final sentence draw?
options: Metrics should be fixed before collecting observations.
Spatial indicators are less useful than passenger interviews.
A useful measurement can mislead when used to answer the wrong question.
Temporary canopies are preferable to long-term planting.
questions.explanation: The same canopy measure was suitable for vegetation coverage but insufficient for passengers’ exposure.

listening.transcript: The shade team asked volunteers to log where people waited, not simply which stop they used. We found that several travellers waited inside a shop doorway and stepped towards the kerb only when the bus was visible. If we had counted people at the pole, those locations would have looked underused. Afterwards, one retailer complained that the study had treated a private doorway as part of the transit system. I think that’s exactly what the result revealed: businesses were taking on a role the transport authority hadn’t provided for. Our recommendation wasn’t to formalise the arrangement. It was to install a shelter where people could wait without relying on a shop being open.

questions.prompt: What pattern would a headcount at the bus-stop pole have hidden?
options: Some riders avoided the bus because railway stations were cooler.
Staff had changed stops without publishing new timetables.
Riders waited nearby until their bus came into view.
Most riders were able to find a seat under an existing shelter.
questions.explanation: Passengers used shop doorways and approached the pole only when needed.

questions.prompt: Why did the retailer object?
options: The survey threatened to close the pavement outside the store.
The survey incorrectly identified the shop as a municipal building.
The shelter would block the shop window.
The study appeared to count private space as transit provision.
questions.explanation: The objection concerned the role attributed to the private doorway.

questions.prompt: How did the speaker interpret the retailer’s objection?
options: It highlighted a service that had informally shifted onto businesses.
It showed that retailers wanted control of public transport.
It justified dropping the stop from the analysis altogether.
It proved that the volunteers had counted the same people twice.
questions.explanation: The objection illustrated how merchants were unintentionally filling a public provision gap.

questions.prompt: What is the intended advantage of the proposed shelter?
options: It would make the shop doorway easier for staff to monitor.
It would provide a waiting place independent of opening hours.
It would move the bus stop nearer the busiest shops.
It would show exactly how long each passenger waited.
questions.explanation: The new waiting space would not depend on whether a shop was open.

writing.prompt: A city has money for only one of two approaches: plant more trees or install shade structures at busy stops. Which would you prioritise and why?
writing.followup: Identify one piece of evidence that could make you change your recommendation.
writing.model: I would install shade structures first at stops where passengers spend the hottest part of the afternoon in direct sunlight. Planting trees is worth doing, but they will not provide dependable cover immediately, and their eventual shade may fall away from the queue. A structure can be positioned and tested against the actual path of the sun. That said, the choice should not favour the busiest stops automatically: a lightly used stop by a clinic may serve people who cannot easily move elsewhere. I would change my recommendation if observations showed that the worst exposure was dispersed across residential walking routes rather than concentrated at stops. In that case, strategically placed trees might benefit more people over time by creating shade along entire routes.

speaking.prompt: Explain why you might choose a different route through a city even if it takes longer.
speaking.followup: How would you persuade a sceptical friend that the longer route is worthwhile?
speaking.model: On a hot afternoon, I choose the river path even though the direct road saves five minutes. Along the river I can stop in the shade, the crossings are calmer, and I arrive less tired. If a friend thought I was just being sentimental about the scenery, I’d suggest walking both routes at the same time on two similar days. We could compare not only the journey times but also how long we spend waiting alongside traffic. Five minutes on a map is a real saving; I just don’t think it’s the only thing worth measuring.

vocab.explanation: This is an invented adjective; stipulate is a real verb meaning to specify a condition.
Intermittent describes something that recurs but does not continue without interruption.
Remedial describes action taken to correct a problem.
The standard verb for compensating someone against loss is indemnify.
The usual spelling of the adjective meaning justifiable is warrantable.
Scrutiny is close or critical examination.

blanks.prompt: The workshop gave an item___ estimate so customers could distinguish labour charges from the cost of parts.
blanks.explanation: An itemised estimate lists individual components and charges.

blanks.prompt: A temporary increase in repeat visits did not substant___ the claim that the repairs were getting worse.
blanks.explanation: To substantiate a claim is to support it with evidence.

reading.passage:
An independent repair workshop introduced a guarantee on labour but not on second-hand parts. The manager had expected customers to reject the distinction. Instead, many welcomed a printed quotation that separated what the workshop controlled from what it could only assess. Customers were more willing to approve a repair once they could see who carried each risk.

A follow-up report appeared to contradict that impression. The number of devices returned after a repair had risen. An accountant interpreted this as evidence of declining workmanship, but the technicians had noticed that people now brought devices back for minor adjustments they would previously have attempted at home. Returns sometimes indicated a greater willingness to ask for help, not a greater likelihood of a defect.

The workshop began recording the reason for each return and whether the original fault had recurred. It kept its limited guarantee rather than expanding it to cover every eventuality. For a business that depended on affordable repairs, an indefinite promise could push prices up and exclude the very people for whom replacing the device was least practical.

questions.prompt: What made customers more prepared to authorise a repair?
options: Evidence that second-hand components rarely fail.
Knowing how the workshop allocated responsibility.
A promise that the quotation price could later be reduced.
A guarantee covering every part regardless of its source.
questions.explanation: The written quotation made the limits of each party’s risk transparent.

questions.prompt: What alternative explanation does the workshop offer for increased returns?
options: Inferior parts were installed more often than before.
The accountant had mistakenly counted returns from a second branch.
Customers who once adjusted devices themselves now sought assistance.
Customers were offered a refund if they reported any inconvenience.
questions.explanation: The guarantee and transparency changed behaviour, so returns do not automatically measure quality.

questions.prompt: Why record whether the original fault had returned?
options: To distinguish a repeat defect from other reasons to seek assistance.
To limit complaint records to claims made within the warranty period.
To train staff to discourage minor follow-up visits.
To create a replacement schedule for all second-hand components.
questions.explanation: Classifying visits makes the repair quality signal more interpretable.

questions.prompt: What consequence does the author associate with indefinite guarantees?
options: Repairers might be compelled to buy only second-hand parts.
Customers might refuse to read written estimates.
Technicians might stop recording why clients return.
Repair prices might rise and deter customers with fewer alternatives.
questions.explanation: The passage highlights a trade-off between breadth of coverage and access.

listening.transcript: When our small repair co-operative started, we advertised that customers would never be charged twice for the same fault. It sounded fair until a tablet began switching off again after three months. The symptom was identical, but this time a new problem had developed in the power connector; our earlier work had addressed a damaged battery. We honoured the promise because customers had no reasonable way to interpret it differently. Then we rewrote the terms. Now we give customers a plain-language description of what we repaired and explain what we will check for free if the problem returns. That distinction is harder to fit on a poster, but easier to honour.

questions.prompt: What made the original promise ambiguous?
options: The same visible symptom could have different underlying causes.
The co-operative had only promised protection on tablets.
It was unclear whether the first repair was authorised.
The tablet had come back after the guarantee period ended.
questions.explanation: The two shutdowns looked alike but originated in different components.

questions.prompt: Why did the co-operative honour the original promise?
options: A court had already ruled that they were responsible.
They accepted how customers would reasonably read it.
They could not locate the technician responsible for the first repair.
They discovered that the original battery had been fitted incorrectly.
questions.explanation: The customer-facing wording gave no clear basis for a narrower interpretation.

questions.prompt: What does the revised guarantee commit to if a problem returns?
options: Replacing the entire device without further investigation.
Offering a partial refund regardless of cause.
Explaining which checks will be carried out at no charge.
Providing free diagnostics for any device bought second-hand.
questions.explanation: The final lines describe free checks specified in plain language.

questions.prompt: What point does the poster comparison illustrate?
options: Visibility is more important than the substance of any warranty.
Promotional promises should always be approved by a lawyer.
Customers now care less about repair guarantees.
A more precise commitment can be less catchy but more practical.
questions.explanation: The speaker contrasts what fits an advertisement with what can reliably be delivered.

writing.prompt: Should repair businesses be required to provide the same guarantees as sellers of new goods? Argue for a rule and explain its trade-offs.
writing.followup: Explain how your rule would handle a fault that looks the same but has a different cause.
writing.model: I would require repair businesses to guarantee their workmanship, but not to offer the same coverage as a seller of new goods. A repairer usually intervenes in one part of a device whose other components may already be close to failure. Making the shop accountable for the whole device would encourage higher prices or the refusal of older items. In exchange for narrower coverage, I would require a written record of what was repaired and a free initial check if the same symptom returns within the guarantee period. If that check identifies a different cause, the shop should explain the distinction and issue a fresh estimate before charging for work. That would preserve consumer protection without making repair an unattractive alternative to replacement.

speaking.prompt: Tell us about an everyday object that is worth repairing rather than replacing. Explain your reasoning.
speaking.followup: What information would you ask a repairer for before deciding?
speaking.model: I would repair my desk lamp. It is heavy enough not to tip, its switch is easy to reach, and the shade directs light exactly where I need it. An apparently cheaper replacement might not do those three things as well. Before agreeing, I’d ask whether the problem is confined to the switch or whether there is also a fault in the wiring. I’d also ask for the cost of the initial inspection and whether it is deducted from the final bill. That tells me what I’m committing to even if the repair turns out not to make sense.

This is not an established verb. To preserve records systematically, use 'archive'.

blanks.explanation: 'Interim' means temporary, pending a final or permanent arrangement.

blanks.prompt: The name in the accession register did not corro___ the family’s account of how the object was acquired.

reading.passage:
When the Alder Municipal Museum announced that three carved panels would be returned to the community that had commissioned them, some trustees called the decision a loss of public access. That objection assumed that access meant the ability of visitors in Alder to stand before the originals. The agreement defined it differently. The recipient museum would decide when the panels could be displayed, but would also run joint workshops with Alder and give researchers access to digitised conservation records. Whether replicas could be made would require a separate decision.

The agreement rested on evidence that was uneven rather than decisive in isolation. Purchase receipts established when the panels entered the collection but said little about who had authorised their removal. Letters in another archive cast doubt on the authority of the intermediary. A community inventory, compiled independently, gave the panels a history that the receipts could not supply. The trustees did not claim to have resolved every uncertainty. Instead, they published the evidence they had and explained what remained disputed. The resulting catalogue entry made an argument about acquisition rather than presenting a date and an owner as sufficient facts.

questions.prompt: What assumption does the second sentence challenge?
options: Only researchers should be allowed to examine museum objects.
Returning an object always makes conservation more difficult.
Public access necessarily means seeing the originals in Alder.
Replicas provide the same experience as the originals.
questions.explanation: The passage contrasts a location-based understanding of access with jointly organised forms of access.

questions.prompt: What did the receipts establish?
options: When the panels joined the collection
That the intermediary was authorised to remove the panels
That the recipient museum had commissioned replicas
Who had originally commissioned each panel
questions.explanation: The receipts documented entry into the collection but not the authority for removal.

questions.prompt: Why is the community inventory important in the trustees’ reasoning?
options: It proved that the receipts had been forged.
It recorded how many visitors had seen the panels.
It identified the party that paid for digitisation.
It added a separately documented history of the objects.
questions.explanation: The inventory was compiled independently and supplemented the ownership information in the receipts.

questions.prompt: What distinguishes the new catalogue entry from a simple inventory listing?
options: It avoids making any claims about ownership.
It interprets the acquisition and identifies unresolved points.
It records only statements accepted by all trustees.
It makes its strongest arguments anonymously.
questions.explanation: The entry explains the reasoning behind the decision and openly identifies disputed matters.

listening.transcript: Before we reopen the east gallery, I want to clarify what the empty case is for. It isn't a memorial to a missing object, nor is it where we'll put a replica. In our trial, visitors often assumed that the object on display had a documented, uncontested route into the collection. This case will invite them to examine a bill of sale and two contradictory accounts of the same transaction. They'll hear an extract from an interview, but the full recording will stay offline at the interviewee's request. Once the initial exhibition ends, we'll collect visitor feedback before deciding whether the empty case should be a permanent feature. Please describe it as a trial in the press materials.

questions.prompt: Why is the museum installing an empty case?
options: To display a replica when a new one is ready
To encourage examination of evidence about an acquisition
To make room for temporary objects arriving later
To honour a donor whose collection was lost
questions.explanation: The case shifts attention to a bill of sale and contradictory accounts of a transaction.

questions.prompt: What did visitors often assume during the trial?
options: The interview had been edited without permission.
The object was too fragile to display.
The museum had borrowed the object from a private collector.
The route into the collection was known and undisputed.
questions.explanation: The speaker says visitors presumed the acquisition route was documented and uncontested.

questions.prompt: Why will the full interview stay offline?
options: The person interviewed requested it.
The staff have not finished transcribing it.
Visitors objected to the recording quality.
The museum cannot confirm who recorded it.
questions.explanation: The limitation was imposed at the interviewee’s request, not for technical reasons.

questions.prompt: What is the staff instruction about publicity?
options: Describe the case as a memorial.
Do not mention the exhibition until feedback arrives.
Present the installation as a trial.
Announce that every future gallery will have an empty case.
questions.explanation: The speaker explicitly asks that press materials call the display a trial.

writing.prompt: A local museum has agreed to return a historically important object. Argue how it should explain that decision to visitors.
writing.followup: Reply to a visitor who says a digital copy is an adequate substitute for the physical object.
writing.model:
The museum should explain its decision beside the former display, not bury it in a press release. A short chronology could show what is known about the acquisition, what remains unclear, and why the board found the case for return persuasive. Giving the receiving institution space to describe its own plans would also prevent the exhibition from implying that the object’s public life has ended.

A digital copy is valuable, particularly for a visitor who cannot travel. It can enlarge details, show historical photographs and connect scattered evidence. Those advantages do not make it equivalent to the original: scale, material and the circumstances in which the object is encountered matter. The best use of a digital copy is therefore to document and interpret the return, not to pretend the return changed nothing.

speaking.prompt: Would an empty display case make you more curious about an absent object? Explain.
speaking.followup: Suggest one practical way to measure whether the display works.
speaking.model: Yes, provided that the case asks a specific question. A label that merely says the object was returned would tell me little. A pair of conflicting records, however, would invite me to work out why the museum changed its interpretation. It would make the decision part of the exhibition rather than administrative background. To test the display, I would ask visitors leaving two comparable galleries to explain one acquisition decision in their own words. I would look for whether they can describe uncertainty accurately, not simply whether they say they liked the exhibition.

title: What the Floating Wetlands Can Do

vocab.explanation: Cloudiness in a liquid caused by suspended particles.
An invented verb. 'Restore a marsh' or 'make an area marshy' would be ordinary alternatives.
Relating to the banks or edges of rivers and streams.
This is not an established noun. 'Root growth' or 'root development' may be appropriate.
This is not an established English word. 'Nutrient sink' describes something that absorbs or stores nutrients.

blanks.prompt: The investigators sampled the upstream site to estab___ a baseline before the installation.
blanks.explanation: 'Establish a baseline' means to create a verified starting point against which later data can be compared.

reading.passage:
The first photographs of Millhaven’s floating wetlands made them look like planted islands. That resemblance was misleading. They were anchored frames supporting plants whose roots hung directly in the water. The project was intended to improve habitat and test whether the plants could remove a meaningful quantity of nutrients from a slow-moving canal. The distinction between those objectives mattered: an installation might attract insects and birds without changing water quality enough for the city to stop controlling pollutants at their source.

Rather than comparing conditions before and after each frame was installed, the researchers added a reference reach without frames. Both reaches experienced heavy rain halfway through the study. Nutrient concentrations fell in both, making a simple before-and-after comparison unreliable. Close to the planted frames, however, samples consistently showed a greater change than samples taken a short distance away. The researchers reported evidence of a local effect but resisted extrapolating to the entire canal. A longer trial would reveal whether roots could retain enough nutrients over more than one growing season and whether harvesting the plants would prevent those nutrients from returning to the water.

questions.prompt: Why does the author distinguish between habitat and water-quality objectives?
options: A habitat benefit would not by itself justify relaxing source controls.
Birds were likely to interfere with water sampling.
The frames could only be installed after pollutants had been eliminated.
A habitat benefit could be identified only through chemical testing.
questions.explanation: The canal can gain wildlife habitat without sufficient nutrient removal to replace pollution control at the source.

questions.prompt: What does the untreated reference reach help investigators account for?
options: Differences between native and non-native plants
Whether visitors understood what they were seeing
The size of the structures needed in a faster current
Other influences on nutrient levels, such as rainfall
questions.explanation: Nutrient levels also fell in the unplanted area after rain, so the decrease could not all be attributed to the frames.

questions.prompt: What does the study provide the strongest evidence for?
options: Identical nutrient removal across the canal
An effect near the frames under the observed conditions
Sustained reductions across multiple growing seasons
Greater long-term returns from frames than from source controls
questions.explanation: The most persuasive differences were close to the frames, and the team did not extrapolate beyond that.

questions.prompt: Why might researchers test the effect of harvesting the plants?
options: To determine whether faster currents could dislodge the frames
To assess whether birds would use the structures in winter
To find out whether stored nutrients can be kept out of the water
To distinguish native plant species from invasive ones
questions.explanation: The passage asks whether removing the plants would prevent retained nutrients from re-entering the canal.

listening.transcript: The grant panel asked whether we could double the number of frames next spring. Technically we could, but that would leave us enough money to inspect them only once a month. Last July a single storm left three frames against the bank, and it took the team half a day to secure them. I'd rather add four frames and pay for weekly checks. Keep two of the new ones unplanted at first: that way we can see how much habitat use has to do with the structure itself, rather than the plants on it. If the inspection records show the design is robust, we can reconsider a larger installation next year.

questions.prompt: Why does the speaker oppose doubling the number of frames immediately?
options: The panel has forbidden additional purchases.
There is no suitable space in the canal.
It would leave too little funding for regular inspections.
The team could not find enough plants.
questions.explanation: The concern is the budget trade-off: doubling installation would restrict inspection to once a month.

questions.prompt: What does the storm example demonstrate?
options: A maintenance problem can occur suddenly and take time to fix.
The plants recovered more quickly than predicted.
Rainfall had no effect on the placement of the frames.
The original design was certified for severe weather.
questions.explanation: One storm displaced three frames and securing them demanded half a day of labour.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of leaving two frames unplanted?
options: To comply with a grant condition on water access
To let maintenance staff practise planting techniques
To assess how quickly the frames degrade
To separate the effect of the frames from the effect of the plants
questions.explanation: Comparing planted and unplanted frames helps distinguish habitat use of the structure from habitat use caused by plants.

questions.prompt: What would justify expanding the project next year?
options: A rise in the number of grant applications
Inspection evidence that the design withstands actual conditions
A decision to abandon the unplanted frames

I would fund a small floating-wetland pilot, but I would not market it as a substitute for controlling pollution. A limited project lets the city learn whether the structures help native species and whether the maintenance bill is manageable. I would compare planted and unplanted frames, inspect them after storms and reserve enough money to remove any structure that fails. The pilot should publish negative results alongside positive ones.

I would expand if repeated observations showed that a variety of native species used the planted frames more than the unplanted ones, without demanding more maintenance than budgeted. I would stop if the frames regularly broke loose during ordinary storms. Even a measurable habitat benefit would not justify an installation that created a predictable hazard for other canal users.

speaking.model: A before-and-after photograph of an urban canal might show an impressive drop in visible algae. I'd want to know whether both photographs were taken in the same season and from the same location. Even honest pictures can highlight changes caused by lighting or weather rather than by a restoration project. I'd ask for regular water-quality readings from the restored canal and from a comparable stretch where no intervention took place. If both improved at the same time, the images might still be useful illustrations, but they'd be much weaker evidence that the restoration caused the change.

Hillwick’s housing advice service trialled four working days without reducing salaries. Teams chose different days off so that the advice line remained open Monday to Friday. Before the trial, the director had promised not to judge the scheme by call counts alone. A team can shorten calls by sending complicated cases to another department, for example, without solving any more problems. The evaluation therefore tracked the share of cases resolved without a second contact and the amount of work sent elsewhere.

Published figures showed a small improvement in first-contact resolution. The headline was favourable, but the average hid a divergence. Teams with shared case records adapted quickly because whoever answered a call could see what colleagues had already done. Teams using separate records spent more time reconstructing the history of individual cases. The trial had not set out to test record systems, and the teams had other differences, including caseload. The evaluators therefore recommended improving access to records and repeating the comparison rather than crediting the working week for every change. For the board, the question was not whether four days worked in the abstract: it was which arrangements made fewer working days possible without shifting costs onto service users or other staff.

That would not tell us everything about workload, but it would show whether the apparent improvement was partly being paid for by colleagues elsewhere.

When Torvale extended the hours of its night market, it measured success by comparing Friday sales before and after the change. Sales rose, but a trader association challenged the measure: customers were also arriving earlier because a concert hall nearby had changed its programme. The association did not dispute that traders were earning more. It disputed the claim that the extended hours had caused the entire increase.

The council redesigned its evaluation. Rather than comparing all Fridays with one another, it monitored equivalent time slots and counted how many purchases occurred after the former closing time. It also surveyed businesses on adjacent streets, where some deliveries had been displaced by a crowded loading bay. To the council's surprise, several businesses reported that adjusted delivery times mattered more than the market's overall footfall.

The experiment did not produce a single verdict. Some traders gained an extra hour of valuable trade; a few reported higher staffing costs than they could justify. The final recommendation was to retain the trial on selected dates while continuing to collect data.

Retailers who profit from evening trade should have the opportunity to test it, but a blanket extension could push costs onto traders whose products attract earlier customers. I would run a six-week trial on alternate Fridays and allow stalls to close at the old time without losing their pitch. To prevent this flexibility from confusing customers, the council could publish a simple map showing which stalls will trade later on each date. It should then compare revenue with staffing and delivery costs, not just count visitors. The trial should become permanent only if the gains survive that broader assessment.

reading.passage:
A neighbourhood archive invited residents to identify people in photographs recovered from an old print shop. Its website initially gave each image a single caption, revised by whoever last submitted an amendment. This seemed efficient until two residents assigned different dates to a photograph of a demolished cinema. Each remembered a different event; both accounts made sense, but neither resident could produce contemporary evidence establishing the date.

The archive could have removed the date altogether. Instead, it split each entry into a stable description and clearly attributed claims. The cinema's location could be corroborated using municipal plans. The date remained disputed, and both explanations were kept visible. An editor could alter the stable description only after recording why. In this way, acknowledging disagreement did not prevent the archive from supplying a usable entry.

The new system did not make every claim equally persuasive. It gave readers the means to see which details rested on contemporary evidence and which depended on later recollection. It also gave contributors a reason to submit overlooked material even when they disagreed with an existing description.

writing.prompt: Should a citizen archive keep competing explanations when their accuracy is uncertain?

writing.model: A citizen archive should preserve competing explanations when their uncertainty is clearly stated. Removing them outright would make some records easier to read, but it would also erase useful clues about what contributors remember and what remains open to investigation. The key distinction is between recording a claim and endorsing it. An entry should first present verifiable details, such as an address that appears on a contemporary map. It should then attribute each disputed interpretation to its source and note any evidence that supports or challenges it. Where consent and privacy permit, readers should also be able to consult the supporting document. This structure protects the archive's reliability without presenting an artificially tidy version of the past.

The council's proposal to turn a former telephone exchange into workshops appeared to have one main economic advantage: the existing building could be acquired cheaply. A cooperative of potential tenants nevertheless objected that this saving would matter little if the converted rooms were too expensive to heat. Its alternative design clustered winter activities on the middle floor rather than insulating the whole building at once.

The architects were initially sceptical. They worried that zoning the heating would bind each organisation to one floor throughout the year. The cooperative replied that the arrangement need not be fixed. A common calendar could show which spaces were heated during a given period and allow tenants to reserve them accordingly. Large spaces on the upper floor would remain available for unheated activities whenever conditions permitted.

A revised cost estimate found that the scheme would be cheaper only if enough tenants agreed to coordinate. The council therefore shifted its attention from capital costs to the practicalities of running the building. In the end, the concept was viable not because the old exchange was cheap to buy, but because prospective users could adapt their routines without substantially compromising their work.

One criterion should therefore be the cost of providing the intended service over a realistic period. The assessment should include maintenance, energy and the availability of accessible space, using schedules supplied by prospective tenants. reading.passage:
A regional council began interpreting its online meetings so that speakers could take part in either of the area's two working languages. Initially, it retained the meeting chair's usual rule: when a speaker finished, the next participant could respond immediately. The interpreters objected that this seemingly neutral rule gave listeners relying on interpretation less time to formulate an answer. A sentence might still be in progress in one language when a participant had already begun reacting to it in the other.

The council tested inserting a pause after every contribution. It soon discovered that equal pauses did not always provide equivalent opportunities to respond. Short remarks seldom needed the full interval; technical exchanges sometimes needed more time than the pause allowed. Chairs were then given a signal indicating that interpretation was complete. Participants could respond after this cue, and the chair could permit a longer interval before moving to a vote.

The test did not remove every disadvantage. Unstable connections still affected whose comments could be heard. It nevertheless revealed that bilingual access depends on meeting rules as well as language provision. A meeting can make interpretation available without giving people a comparable chance to use it.

It prevented chairs from reading technical papers
questions.explanation: Responses could begin while some listeners were still hearing the first contribution.

options: Remarks differed in how much time interpretation and response required
Participants refused to accept any interruption
Interpretation stopped whenever a pause began
Chairs used different clocks
questions.explanation: A fixed interval could be unnecessarily long or too short.

options: It warned the chair of weak connections

It indicated that interpretation had finished
questions.explanation: The cue let chairs start the response period after interpretation.

If a word seems to have been mistranslated, type the original term and the time you heard it in the meeting chat. Don't post a corrected translation without identifying the term. The chair will review those comments during the scheduled break. We'll stop immediately only if the interpretation channel goes quiet for several people or if the interruption affects a formal vote.

writing.followup: Propose one test that could show whether people can participate on comparable terms.
writing.model: Online consultations can remove travel barriers, but their value depends on how organisers structure participation. A translated statement is not enough if the people listening to it receive the information just as the chair closes the discussion. I would run two otherwise similar pilot sessions. In one, the chair would use fixed intervals. In the other, the chair would wait for an interpretation-complete signal before taking responses. Participants would then be asked whether they had enough time to formulate a question, and organisers would record how many people in each language requested and received a turn. A fairer procedure would narrow the difference without making discussion impractically slow.

speaking.prompt: Describe a misunderstanding that can occur in an online meeting.
speaking.followup: Explain a practical way to prevent it without interrupting everyone repeatedly.
speaking.model: A familiar misunderstanding occurs when the chair asks whether anyone objects and takes silence as agreement. Some participants may still be finding the right control or working out what the proposal means. I would replace the open-ended question with a brief recorded response: support, object or abstain. For ordinary discussions, the chair could post the proposal in the chat and allow a short reading period. This would make silence less ambiguous without requiring frequent interruptions, and anyone who missed the question could refer back to the written wording.
